SIS / ISIS screening for high dimensional models

Source: vignettes/articles/high-dimensional.Rmd
high-dimensional.Rmd

SIS stands for Sure Independence Screening and ISIS for Iterative Sure Independence Screening. These methods rapidly prescreen the most promising predictors, after which L0glm performs joint sparse selection and estimation. This combination gives excellent stability in high dimensional examples and scales well to very large predictor sets. SIS was introduced by Fan & Lv (2008), and Fan, Samworth & Wu (2009) developed the general likelihood-based ISIS framework. L0glm uses an offset-based screen followed by joint sparse refitting; the controls are documented in sisGLM().

ISIS is enabled by default for ultrahigh-dimensional models through screen="auto". Let n be the number of observations and p_{\mathrm{eligible}} the number of eligible predictors, excluding mandatory terms and predictors excluded by zero starts in every response channel. Automatic ISIS is enabled when

p_{\mathrm{eligible}}>10n.

The same rule applies in l0glmTune(), independently for each full-data or CV training fit, using its training row count. There is no separate minimum sample size or predictor count.

Screening keeps the full fitting interface while concentrating joint fitting on a small, informative candidate set. Use screen="ISIS" to request it explicitly at any design size.

SIS or ISIS in one call

screen="SIS" performs one marginal screen. screen="ISIS" repeats screening against the current model, incorporating its predictions as offsets, and keeps the best joint-fitting round. screen="auto" enables ISIS for ultrahigh-dimensional designs. screen="none" fits the supplied design directly.

set.seed(31)
X <- matrix(rnorm(250*5000), 250, 5000)
beta <- numeric(5000); beta[c(5, 50, 500)] <- c(2, -1.5, 1)
y <- as.numeric(X %*% beta) + rnorm(250)
fit <- l0glmFit(X, y, family=gaussian(), lambda="gic",
  screen="ISIS", screen.nthreads=2L, relaxed=TRUE)
l0glmMetrics(fit, beta_true=beta)[c("gic", "TP", "FP", "FN", "TN", "F1_score", "MCC")]
#>   gic TP FP FN   TN F1_score MCC
#> 1 797  3  0  0 4997        1   1

nsis controls a SIS retained set or an ISIS batch. The default ISIS batch is GIC-based. A small batch lets joint fitting remove false positives as the search progresses. Screening is implemented in Rcpp with OpenMP and supports ordinary GLMs, negative binomial, multinomial and Cox models.

fit$screening records selected predictors, screening rounds, elapsed time and thread use. By default screening uses all physical cores, with one thread as the fallback when detection is unavailable. Explicit screen.nthreads values remain available. Coefficients always have the original dimensions, with zeros for predictors excluded by screening.

A million-variable example

This simulation has 500 observations, one million standard-normal predictors and 60 nonzero effects of either sign. The dense design occupies about 4 GB.

n <- 500L
p <- 1000000L
set.seed(123)
X <- matrix(rnorm(n*p), n, p)
active <- sample.int(p, 60L)
beta <- numeric(p)
beta[active] <- runif(60L, -.8, .8)
set.seed(1)
y <- as.numeric(X[, active] %*% beta[active]) + rnorm(n)

fit <- l0glmFit(X, y, family=gaussian())
l0glmMetrics(fit, beta_true=beta)[c("gic", "TP", "FP", "FN", "TN", "F1_score", "MCC")]

The default L0glm fit with ISIS recovers 40 true effects with 2 false positives in 2.84 s using eight physical cores. Five-fold-CV LASSO on the unscreened design takes 120.69 s and recovers 17 true effects with 50 false positives. The benchmark article gives the tuning settings.

Compare screening and complete models with SIS

On a Gaussian design with 500 observations and one million predictors, sisGLM() and SIS returned identical complete screening ranks, including the same top 100 predictors. Screening-only median timings over three runs:

Screening routine Seconds
sisGLM(), eight physical cores 0.24
sisGLM(nthreads=1) 0.80
SIS Gaussian screen (obtain.ix0) 2.03

The SIS row calls its screening helper directly, excluding the subsequent LASSO fit. Gaussian correlation ranks are scale invariant, so redundant standardization is omitted. The OpenMP screen is 8.5 times faster on this machine.

Complete screening-and-selection pipelines were timed separately on the same million-predictor simulation as the homepage. L0glm uses its default GIC preset. LASSO variants use BIC-selected paths because GIC commonly selects an empty LASSO model in this example. The comparisons below set local.search=FALSE to isolate screening and adaptive ridge; the opening example uses the automatic final refinement. The one-pass comparison retains 100 predictors. On the million-predictor design, ISIS uses the default GIC-based batch size and ten rounds. The SIS-package ISIS comparison uses a separate 5,000-predictor design and three rounds; nsis=100 is a batch size in L0glm and a total support limit in SIS. Standalone l0glmFit() retains its best ISIS round by GIC; the LASSO comparisons use the requested BIC for their outer searches. The public SIS pipeline fits a free intercept; L0glm and glmnet use a zero intercept, matching the simulation. Both ICs are saved with the results.

The rows below report median elapsed time over three runs. They include screening and variable selection for each fitted model.

sparseGLM() also supports screen="SIS", "ISIS", "auto" and "none" for every compatible method. Each ISIS search uses its own method’s fitted predictions as screening offsets. CV recomputes screening on training rows, and returned coefficients retain every original predictor row.

comparison <- sparseGLM(X, y,
  method=c("L0glm", "abess", "lasso", "relaxed_lasso"),
  screen="ISIS", nsis=10, tune="gic", nlambda=10,
  lambda=list(L0glm=presetLambda("gic", ncol(X), nrow(X))),
  options=list(L0glm=list(relaxed=TRUE)), beta_true=beta)
l0glmMetrics(comparison)[c("method", "screen", "seconds", "gic",
  "TP", "FP", "F1_score", "MCC")]

HP ZBook Fury G8 Mobile Workstation, Intel Core i9-11950H, eight physical cores / 16 logical cores; R 4.5.0, SIS 1.5, one BLAS thread. Timings exclude data generation. The sparseGLM rows include common candidate scoring and diagnostics. The sisGLM() example and benchmark script give the calls and checks.

GIC tuning and cross-validation 

gic <- l0glmTune(X, y, family=gaussian(), screen="ISIS",
  screen.nthreads=8L, tune="gic", nlambda=10, relaxed=TRUE)
cv <- l0glmTune(X, y, family=gaussian(), screen="ISIS",
  screen.nthreads=8L, tune="cv", nfolds=5, nlambda=10, relaxed=TRUE)

Each fold screens its training observations independently. Validation can also compare a batch grid, for example nsis=c(2L, 5L, 10L) with validation=list(X=V, y=v), while retaining the default GIC batch when nsis=NULL.
